passage:
Dear Ritu Didi,
Thank you for the photo of Nana at your wedding. I've stuck it inside my maths notebook.
It's been three months. Some days I'm fine, and then a song on the bus hits me like a wave. I get angry too: at the hospital, at Nana for not telling us he felt ill, at myself for skipping his birthday call to finish a game.
Yesterday Isha showed me a silly video in the library and I laughed out loud. Then I felt terrible, as if laughing meant I'd forgotten him.
Mum says laughing is allowed. We talk about Nana every Sunday over his favourite jalebi.
You asked me to tell you if the sad feeling spreads to everything. Right now it's mostly about Nana. I still like drawing and my friends. If that changes, I'll tell Mum and the school counsellor. Promise.
Love,
Nikita

qa.q: Where did Nikita stick the photo of Nana?
qa.a: Inside Nikita's maths notebook.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel terrible after laughing in the library?
qa.a: Nikita felt ashamed, as if laughing meant Nana had been forgotten.

qa.q: What choice has Nikita made in case the sadness spreads, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Nikita has promised to tell Mum and the school counsellor if the sadness spreads to everything, so help would come early.

qa.q: How might Ritu Didi feel reading that the sadness is still mostly about Nana?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that Nikita still enjoys drawing and friends, while staying ready to help if that changes.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose grief for a grandparent brings sadness, anger, guilt and ashamed laughter, still tied to the loss and eased by family support.

passage: People think the year after someone dies is just sad. For me it was messy. I'm Vandana, and Jagdish Sir coached our kabaddi team from the time I was eleven. When he died in the bus accident, I was angry first, at the driver, at the rain, at myself for sulking through our last practice instead of saying thanks. Then in our first match without him, I made a raid, the whole team screamed, and I laughed. On the ride home I felt sick with shame, like I'd betrayed him. For a while it was only about him, and I could carry that. But around March I stopped caring about anything, even drawing, and I kept thinking I was useless. My mum noticed I'd stopped eating with the family and booked a counsellor that same week. That helped a lot. Now when I laugh on the mat, I think he'd have laughed too.

qa.q: Which sport did Jagdish Sir coach?
qa.a: Kabaddi.

qa.q: Why did Vandana feel sick with shame on the ride home?
qa.a: Vandana had laughed after a raid in the first match without Jagdish Sir and felt that the laughter betrayed him.

qa.q: What was the turning point around March, and why did it matter?
qa.a: When Vandana stopped caring about anything and felt useless, Mum noticed and booked a counsellor that same week, getting help before things got worse.

qa.q: How might Vandana's mum have seen the change around March?
qa.a: She likely saw that it was no longer only grief for Jagdish Sir but a sadness spreading into everything, so she acted quickly.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose grief for a coach mixes anger, guilt and ashamed laughter, and whose family seeks help when the sadness spreads to everything.

Vasudha: and then I felt sick. like how can I laugh when papa's gone
Anand: it's allowed. you didn't forget him
Vasudha: yesterday I was so angry I kicked the bin. angry at the hospital. angry at him for not going to the doctor sooner

Anand: then I think you're grieving, not broken. but if it ever turns grey all over, tell me and we'll go to the counsellor together

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel after laughing at the video?

passage: Six months after his cousin Uday died in a tractor accident, Baljeet, sixteen, laughed at a wedding in the village. A friend had tripped over a rope, and everybody roared. Then Baljeet stopped, cold. How could he laugh? He walked behind the tent, face hot with shame. Some days he was furious, at the tractor, at the muddy road, even at Uday for driving too fast. Other days he felt guilty that he hadn't gone with him. His Bebe found him behind the tent. "Laughing doesn't mean you forgot Uday. He would have laughed the loudest." Baljeet's eyes filled. He still went to kabaddi practice, still helped in the fields. The grief came in waves, but it hadn't swallowed everything.

qa.q: How did Uday die?
qa.a: Uday died in a tractor accident.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel after laughing at the wedding?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and cold, as if laughing meant forgetting Uday.

qa.q: What did Bebe say that helped Baljeet?
qa.a: She told him laughing did not mean he forgot Uday, and that Uday would have laughed loudest.

qa.q: How might Bebe have felt finding Baljeet behind the tent?
qa.a: She was likely sad herself but tender, wanting to ease his shame.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose grief brings sadness, anger, guilt and shame at laughing, still tied to the loss and eased by support.

passage: In a Madrid school yard, Sofia, sixteen, sat on the wall while her friends played music. Her grandmother had died in October. Some mornings Sofia was fine; some mornings she cried in the bathroom before maths. Yesterday she'd yelled at her mother for throwing out her grandmother's old coat, then felt awful. Today a joke made her laugh, and straight away she felt guilty. Jin, her friend from the art club, sat beside her. "Are you still painting?" "Every evening. It's the only time I feel okay." "Then keep painting. And if it ever feels like nothing is okay, not even painting, will you tell the counsellor?" Sofia nodded. "I miss her so much." Jin just stayed beside her.

qa.q: When did Sofia's grandmother die?
qa.a: She died in October.

qa.q: How did Sofia feel after laughing at the joke?
qa.a: She felt guilty right away, as if she shouldn't laugh while grieving.

qa.q: Why does Jin ask whether Sofia is still painting?
qa.a: To check whether the sadness is still tied to the loss rather than spreading to everything, and to encourage the counsellor if it does.

qa.q: How might Sofia's mother have felt when Sofia yelled about the coat?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt but understood that Sofia was grieving and angry about losing her grandmother.

grounding: Shows a teenager grieving in waves of sadness, anger and guilty laughter, tied to the loss and eased by a friend, with help sought if sadness spreads.

passage:
Two months after her brother Manpreet died in the road accident, Gurpreet was back at school. At lunch in the canteen, Wasim did his funny impression of the PT teacher, and Gurpreet laughed out loud. Then she stopped, cheeks burning. How could she laugh?
In the counsellor's room that afternoon, she said it all. "Some days I'm so angry at him for riding in the rain. Then I feel guilty for being angry. And today I laughed."
Mrs D'Souza listened. "Grief comes in waves. Laughing doesn't mean you loved him less. It sounds like the sadness is still about Manpreet, and you still enjoy hockey and your friends."
Gurpreet nodded.
"If the sadness starts spreading to everything, or you feel worthless, come and tell me that same day. We'll keep meeting every Friday."

qa.q: What was Wasim doing when Gurpreet laughed?
qa.a: His funny impression of the PT teacher.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel right after laughing?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and guilty, her cheeks burning, as if laughing meant she didn't care about her brother.

qa.q: What did Mrs D'Souza do that supported Gurpreet?
qa.a: She listened, explained that grief comes in waves and laughter is okay, set regular meetings and told her what signs would need extra attention.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel if he knew why Gurpreet stopped laughing?
qa.a: He might feel awkward or worried he'd upset her, though he probably helped her by bringing a moment of lightness.

grounding: Gurpreet feels sadness, anger, guilt and shame at laughing after her brother's death, and a counsellor explains grief's waves and when it needs more attention.
